tldr: When signs of failure appear during humanoid acrobatics, instead of falling immediately, this method uses a three-tier hierarchical selection (VAPS) that introduces an "abort to feet" option. This minimizes damage risk to the head and hands while maximizing task success rate.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed VAPS framework. (a) Pre-train three specialist policies: nominal tracking, abort, and protective fall. (b) Train viability predictors to estimate whether each policy can remain viable within a finite horizon. (c) During real robot deployment, sequentially select and switch to the least-sacrificial viable policy.
overview:
Dynamic acrobatic motions like flips by humanoid robots are impressive when successful. However, slight disturbances or sim-to-real gaps can knock them off track, causing severe impacts that destroy expensive sensors and joints. Conventional safety mechanisms have mostly offered a binary choice: continue the nominal motion or switch to a protective fall. Yet in high-speed motions like flips, hardware still suffers critical damage even with a protective fall. In reality, a clear intermediate zone exists before falling: when completing the acrobatics is impossible, the robot can still stop rotating and land on its feet (an abort).

The authors realized that safety does not depend solely on robot state; it depends on which policy runs next and how much time remains. Based on this, they proposed Viability-Aware Policy Selection (VAPS). VAPS prepares three specialist policies: Nominal, Abort, and Protective Fall. A predictor monitors at every step whether each policy can survive over a short look-ahead horizon (Viability). It then selects the least-sacrificial policy among the viable choices—giving up as little of the task objective as possible.

Through cartwheel and front-flip experiments in simulation (Unitree G1 and LimX Oli) and on real hardware (LimX Oli), VAPS dramatically reduced head contact rates compared to a single fall backup. In the Pareto trade-off between task success and safety, it outperformed both end-to-end learning and distilled policies.
contributions: Proposed VAPS, a hierarchical policy selection framework based on the least-sacrificial safety principle, comprising three tiers: continue, abort to feet, and protective fall.
Constructed a mechanism that evaluates policy-conditioned, receding-horizon viability at every step using learned predictors based on proprioceptive history.
Extensively benchmarked against monolithic alternatives such as single-network reinforcement learning and imitation distillation (DAgger), showing that VAPS Pareto-dominates them.
Validated in simulation on the Unitree G1 and LimX Oli, and demonstrated sim-to-real transfer of both the viability predictors and the full VAPS controller for side-flip motions on the real LimX Oli.

sections.heading: Fall right after a slip? Acrobatics needs a third choice: abort
sections.summary: Humanoid acrobatic motions last only 1 to 2 seconds. Once off the reference, there is no time to recover to the original trajectory. Yet rather than falling right away, there is often room to stop in mid-air and land on the feet. This calls for fine-grained interventions tailored to the situation.
sections.details:
Humanoid acrobatic skills are typically learned by tracking policies that follow human motion capture data. However, tracking policies never experience off-reference states during training. Once destabilized by disturbances or sim-to-real gaps, they cannot recover on their own.

Most existing safety mechanisms rely on an all-or-nothing binary choice: keep nominal control or hand over to a safety shield or fall policy. But in high-speed maneuvers like flips, robots sustain serious damage even when executing a clean protective fall. Even if a motion begins to break down, a gray zone often remains where the robot can cancel the flip and land on its feet instead of dropping straight to the ground.

To tackle this, the authors took the viewpoint that whether a state is safe depends on which closed-loop controller runs next. They structured a policy hierarchy with varying degrees of task sacrifice—nominal, abort, and fall—and proposed VAPS, which assesses short-term viability at every control step to pick the optimal policy.

sections.heading: How VAPS differs from prior safety controls: when, what, and how to switch
sections.summary: Prior work spans acrobatic generation, protective falls, intervention triggers, and architecture design. Prior methods usually route to a single backup using a single safety value, or combine everything into one policy. VAPS sets itself apart by pairing multiple specialist policies with policy-conditioned predictors.
sections.details:
Safety architectures for dynamic motions can be structured into four components: motion generator, protective maneuver, intervention trigger, and intervention composition.

- Acrobatic generation: Reinforcement learning via imitation has achieved diverse aerial maneuvers, but handling trajectory deviations during deployment is rarely addressed.
- Protective and recovery maneuvers: Protective fall policies minimizing impact forces have been proposed, but these activate only after a fall is certain; landing on feet to avoid falling altogether is not considered.
- Intervention triggers: Control barrier functions (CBFs), constrained critics, and fall predictors typically compute a single safety index for one policy. They cannot measure fine-grained severity, such as whether nominal control failed but landing on the feet is still possible.
- Intervention composition: Prior setups mostly feature binary handovers from a nominal policy to a single backup, or pack everything into a single monolithic network. However, monolithic policies struggle with trade-offs between dynamic maneuvers and protective goals.

In contrast, VAPS keeps nominal execution as a black box, introduces two backups with different objectives (abort and protective fall), monitors the viability of each policy continuously, and switches hierarchically.

sections.heading: Designing VAPS: three specialists, viability predictors, and least sacrifice
sections.summary: VAPS consists of three specialist policies (nominal, abort, protective fall), viability predictors estimating the probability of avoiding a fall over a horizon, and a least-sacrificial selection rule. It also examines whether a single network could replace this modular structure.
sections.details:
The VAPS algorithm rests on three core elements alongside a comparison against single-network variants:

### III-A Specialist Policies
Safe acrobatic execution is decomposed into three independent policies:
- Nominal policy ($\pi_{\mathrm{nom}}$): Strictly tracks the reference trajectory. Episodes terminate immediately upon deviation during training, so it has no recovery ability from failure states.
- Abort policy ($\pi_{\mathrm{abort}}$): Discards the reference and aims to stand upright with both soles grounded. It is trained initialized from a transition dataset generated by perturbing the nominal policy.
- Protective fall policy ($\pi_{\mathrm{protect}}$): Intervenes when a fall is unavoidable. It breaks the fall while minimizing joint torques and contact forces on sensitive regions like the head ($c_{\mathrm{head}}$) and hands ($c_{\mathrm{hand}}$).

### III-B Policy-Conditioned, Receding-Horizon Viability
Viability $V_i^H(s_t)$ is defined as the probability that executing policy $\pi_i$ from state $s_t$ does not lead to a failure $F$ (non-foot body contact with the ground) within $H$ future steps. A neural network $f_{\theta_i}$ is trained using the past $N$ steps of proprioceptive history. To prioritize near-term errors, it is optimized via cross-entropy loss with a geometric discount rate $\gamma$.

### III-C Viability-Aware Policy Selection (VAPS)
Task priority follows the order: Nominal (full task) > Abort (upright landing) > Protective fall. At runtime, VAPS executes the policy with the highest task priority among those whose predicted viability exceeds a threshold (Eq. 11). If the nominal policy is deemed unsafe ($V_{\mathrm{nom}}^H \le \tau_{\mathrm{nom}}$), it evaluates the abort policy; if that is also unviable, it drops straight to the protective fall. If the abort predictor flags danger during an abort, it escalates to a protective fall.

### III-D Single-Network Alternatives
To test whether this modular design can be collapsed into one network, the authors built an end-to-end RL policy with protective rewards and a distilled policy trained via DAgger on oracle-routed VAPS decisions for comparison.

sections.heading: Simulation and real-robot tests: striking head protection and Pareto dominance
sections.summary: Experiments were run on Unitree G1 front-flips and LimX Oli side-flips. VAPS viability predictors detected anomalies earlier than baseline fall predictors and worked accurately on the real robot. VAPS Pareto-dominated end-to-end and distilled models, and also proved effective at safeguarding partially trained policies.
sections.details:
VAPS modules and overall performance were tested in simulation and on real hardware:

### IV-A & IV-B Specialist Robustness and Viability Prediction Accuracy
Under increased disturbances where nominal policy success plummeted to 15%, the abort policy still achieved upright landings in 62% of trials, and the protective fall prevented head contact in 96% of cases (Table I). This confirms a wide viable window exists where safe abort is possible after nominal tracking fails.
Furthermore, compared to a SafeFall-style baseline (predicting falls at episode termination), the VAPS viability predictor achieved higher detection rates at the same low false-alarm rate (under 1%). It issued alerts 30–60% earlier (more than 0.5 s in advance) (Table II). In 13 real-robot side-flip tests on the LimX Oli, it detected failures an average of 0.544 s before impact with zero false alarms (Fig. F3).

### IV-C System-Level Evaluation and Hardware Experiments
In ablation tests on the Unitree G1 (Table III), an abort-only setup (Nominal–Abort) had a low fall rate, but its head contact rate upon failure reached 5.0%. In contrast, full VAPS held head contact to 1.6% while cutting the fall rate to 26.2%. The compute time for policy switching was just 0.29 ms on a single CPU core (1.45% of the control step).
On the real LimX Oli, manual switching tests saw the abort policy stick an upright landing in 17 of 19 trials, while the protective fall protected the head and hands in 12 of 16 trials. In autonomous intervention tests of the full VAPS framework, 15 of 18 trials (83.3%) met their intended safety targets.

### IV-D Comparison with Single-Policy Alternatives
Against end-to-end RL and DAgger-distilled policies (Fig. 4), single networks failed to balance task success and head protection. VAPS completely Pareto-dominated them on the Pareto frontier. Single networks struggled to learn sharp decision boundaries for when to give up on the task.

### IV-E Supervising Under-Trained Policies
Applying VAPS to intermediate checkpoints (16 training stages) of the nominal policy kept head contact near zero throughout training without compromising task success rates.

sections.heading: Summary and outlook: the art of giving up unlocks safe robotics
sections.summary: Guided by the idea that state safety depends on the next action and remaining time, the authors proposed VAPS with three-tier least-sacrificial selection. This explicit structure is hard to replicate in a single network, holding promise for safe deployment across diverse dynamic tasks beyond acrobatics.
sections.details:
While humanoids continue to gain advanced athletic skills, safe deployment without breaking hardware has lagged behind. VAPS emerged from the insight that safety is not an isolated state property; it depends on what is executed next and how much time is left.

By placing an "abort to feet" option between nominal continuation and protective falling, and continuously assessing finite-horizon viability to switch with least sacrifice, VAPS demonstrated superior safety and task performance that end-to-end models cannot match.

This modular architecture applies not only to disturbance rejection for mature controllers, but also to protecting undertrained policies and handling external e-stop requests. Knowing when to give up on a task and how to abort safely will become an essential question for all future autonomous robots, well beyond acrobatics.

takeaways: Safety is not a property of the robot state alone; it depends on the closed-loop behavior of which policy runs next.
Rather than dropping straight into a fall when acrobatics fail, adding an abort specialist that lands on the feet drastically cuts hardware damage.
Attempting to unify safety and task execution into a single neural network often fails; an explicit modular design with specialist policies and viability predictors holds a clear advantage.
Training viability predictors on the actual handover state distribution where switches occur is critical for prediction accuracy.
limitations: Hardware testing was limited to 18 trials, meaning more real-robot runs are required for statistically rigorous validation of false-alarm rates.
State transitions are strictly one-way (Nominal → Abort → Fall); once an abort triggers, there is no path back to resuming the acrobatics even if the trajectory stabilizes.
The abort policy assumes flat ground for landing; validation on rough terrain or cluttered environments with obstacles was not covered.
